question: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionising recruitment processes by providing tools that find, assess and select candidates with unprecedented efficiency. This technology makes it easier to evaluate CVs, conduct pre-hiring assessments and even predict how successful a candidate will be within an organisation and how well they will fit in.

Despite these advances, there is a growing concern about algorithm bias (AI bias), which is liable to perpetuate discrimination and undermine fairness in the recruitment process. Since it is important to ensure fair and flawless hiring processes, it is vital to address the challenges associated with algorithm bias in AI-led recruitment.
I would therefore like to ask the Commission to clarify its position and what action it has taken. 1.
What measures or initiatives has the Commission taken to address algorithm bias in AI recruitment tools?
How does the AI Act provide for mitigating bias in AI recruitment applications, thereby ensuring fair hiring practices?
Could the Commission provide details of the guidelines or resources available to the developers and users of AI recruitment technologies so as to promote their ethical use and prevent discrimination?
answer: 1. The Commission aims to create a European ecosystem for trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) and is paying attention to algorithmic bias in areas such as recruitment. The 2020 White Paper on AI (1) highlighted discrimination as one of the potential risks of AI.

Since then, the Commission has taken several initiatives to address algorithm bias in recruitment, including by assigning studies and reports (2), holding seminars (3) and with its proposal for an AI Act (4) formally adopted by the Council on 21 May 2024.

The Commission has also proposed legislation to ensure that equality bodies have the necessary resources to assess the compliance of AI systems with non-discrimination law (5). 2. Certain AI systems in the area of employment will be classified as high-risk under the AI Act and will need to be developed in accordance with requirements for trustworthy AI.

The latter address numerous causes of algorithmic bias, including biased training data. Training data sets will be subject to appropriate data management practices, including an examination in view of possible biases and appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate identified biases. Training data must be relevant and representative to ensure that typical causes of bias effects are eliminated.

The required human oversight aims at fair and non-discriminatory decision-making. 3. The Commission is now preparing guidelines on high-risk AI systems that will be available before the AI Act becomes applicable.

At the same time, the Commission, in close collaboration with the Member States in consultation with stakeholders, will develop an ecosystem in which operators of AI recruitment technologies will receive support and resources for the development of ethical AI (6).
